body: President Donald Trump recommended that Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky nominate someone else to negotiate a peace deal with Russia .

Trump made the recommendation Monday as he departed the White House for a campaign rally in Kansas. The comments came in response to a question about Zelensky saying Trump is on the “wrong side of history” for Washington’s approach to peace talks.

“Zelensky doesn’t know what he’s talking about,” Trump said. “Zelensky is a man that should have had this war settled a long time ago. If he would have listened to me, he would have made a much better deal a long time ago, and he’d have a million people living from his side.”
“To be honest, I think that it’s time for somebody else to negotiate on behalf of Ukraine,” the president added. “Maybe it’s time for Zelensky to get somebody else to negotiate.”
Trump defended his decision to strike a diesel deal with Russia and ease sanctions on Moscow, despite criticism from Republicans that he is siding with Russian President Vladimir Putin over Zelensky.

“I’m trying to get a hostage,” Trump said. “We also have a very good situation with respect to Iran [and Russia]. [Putin’s] laying off Iran. It’s nice because we’re hitting Iran very hard, as you know, economically as well as militarily, and Russia has done nothing there that we can see. I think that’s very positive, and of course we’re negotiating with him on Ukraine.”
He continued, “I’m supporting stopping war between Russia and Ukraine … Frankly, Zelensky is not helping matters much. I think he doesn’t want to stop it, but I want to see people not die.”

At the same time, Trump downplayed speculation of a trilateral meeting between him, Putin, and Chinese President Xi Jinping when he travels to China in November. Trump also said a separate sit-down with North Korean dictator Kim Jong Un might not be in the books.
ZACHARIA OUSTER RAISES QUESTION ABOUT IMPORTANCE OF THE WHITE HOUSE PRESS SECRETARY

“We would have him to talk about nuclear weapons and denuclearization,” he said of the Putin-Xi summit, adding that trade would be on the agenda as well. “It’ll take about probably five years. We would schedule a meeting based on the denuclearization, and that’s a very positive thing for the world.”
On whether he would use that opportunity to talk with Putin about Ukraine without Zelensky, Trump said he would do “anything … to end the war, whether somebody’s there or not.”

articles.headline: Slick Abdul
keyFacts: Michigan Senate candidate Abdul el Sayed denied ties to the Muslim Brotherhood after Republican Mike Rogers accused him of having connections.
The Washington Free Beacon reported social media posts by el Sayed's half-sister describing family involvement with the Muslim Brotherhood.
During a town hall meeting in Caro, Michigan, el Sayed challenged an attendee who asked if he disavowed the Muslim Brotherhood.
body: SLICK ABDUL. Over the weekend, a video featuring Michigan Democratic Senate candidate Abdul el Sayed went viral on social media. In it, a young man who attended an el Sayed town hall in Caro, Michigan, asked if the candidate disavowed the Muslim Brotherhood .

It was a reasonable question. In recent weeks, el Sayed’s Republican opponent, Mike Rogers, had accused el Sayed of having ties to the Muslim Brotherhood, of which several branches have been designated terrorist organizations by the U.S. government, including the branch in Egypt, where el Sayed’s family came from. In an Oct. 11 appearance on NBC News’s Meet the Press , moderator Kristen Welker said to el Sayed: “For Michigan voters, who are hearing those attacks against you, who are looking to separate fact from fiction, can you set the record straight about whether you or your family have any ties to the Muslim Brotherhood?”

“No, but let’s talk about this,” el Sayed responded. In context, what el Sayed meant by “no” was unclear, so Welker asked, “No, you don’t have any ties?” El Sayed responded: “No.” Then Welker asked, “And your family doesn’t?” El Sayed responded, “No. Let me ask you, though, why this is even a subject of debate? Because [Rogers’s] only strategy is to point to me and my name and my faith and to say that we’re different. And that you should suspect people simply because they are different than you in how they pray.”

The interview moved on to other topics. But later that Sunday, the Washington Free Beacon published a story based on social media posts by el Sayed’s half sister in 2012 and 2013. Back then, the Washington Free Beacon reported, “Eman Abdelhadi, [now] an assistant professor at the University of Chicago, wrote openly about her family’s ties to the Muslim Brotherhood.”

The Washington Free Beacon offered examples: “‘My family has long been MB,’ Abdelhadi wrote on June 24, 2012, days after Egypt elected Muslim Brother leader Mohamed Morsi as president. ‘I have had family jailed for being part of it,’ she wrote on July 3, 2013. ‘Praying for all my family that supports that #MB in Egypt. Lie low, stay safe,’ she said.”

That certainly cast a different light on el Sayed’s interview on Meet the Press . A few days later, NBC questioned el Sayed about the posts from Abdelhadi reported in the Washington Free Beacon , plus one more that said, “Had an amazing talk with my mom about her activism in the Muslim Brotherhood during the early ’70s while she was in college. Hashtag respect.” During the new NBC interview, el Sayed tried to tell reporter Tom Llamas that it was all nothing.

“Yeah, Tom, it’s funny to me,” he said. “I was born in 1984, down the street in Rochester Hills. I was raised here in Michigan, went to the University of Michigan, rebuilt the health department in the city, led the health department in this county. And you want to ask me about what’s happening in Egypt in 1970? Are you serious?”
“I get it, but you were asked a question, and you gave an answer,” said Llamas. El Sayed responded, “This is kind of like the same — yeah, I’m telling you, I have no ties. We have no ties.”
“So your mother had no ties?” Llamas asked. El Sayed answered: “I have never had these conversations with my mother. I wasn’t raised by my mother.” Then Llamas pressed: “So you’re unaware?”
El Sayed did not answer. Instead, he said, “But I’m just telling you that you’re using hearsay evidence from a tweet. This is not serious. It’s not serious.”

“Correct,” Llamas said. “But you’ve also gone after the president for truthfulness. You’ve also gone after the president for truthfulness. So when people ask you a question, they all do expect the truth.”
“And do you think, are you insinuating that somehow I was lying?” el Sayed asked. “I don’t know — that’s why I’m asking,” said Llamas. “And I’m telling you, I was not,” el Sayed said.

So what is the truth? A reasonable conclusion would be that it is hard to say. But that is where things stood on Saturday when el Sayed arrived at his town hall in Caro. There, a young man named Tommy — later identified as Thomas Teepell, a former staffer for Sen. Josh Hawley (R-MO) — yelled out , “Abdul! Will you disavow the Muslim Brotherhood?”

“What’s your name?” el Sayed responded. Teepell said, “It’s a simple question.” The two went back and forth for a while as el Sayed refused to answer until Tommy identified himself. “You give me your name, I’ll answer the question,” el Sayed said. “OK, Tommy,” Teepell said.

After a quick how-are-you, el Sayed moved on to misdirection. “Do you know what the Constitution of the United States is?” he asked Teepell. Young Tommy did not bite. “I have one simple question,” he said. “Will you disavow the Muslim Brotherhood?”

“Sure, yeah, absolutely, but I want to ask to the question that you’re asking,” el Sayed said. “Why are you asking the question?” “Well, because they’re a terrorist group,” Teepell answered. El Sayed responded, “OK, no, no, but what are you implying? Do you assume that I wouldn’t?”
“Yes,” said Teepell. “Why not?” asked el Sayed. “Because I have not heard you disavow them yet,” Teepell answered.

At that point the exchange had reached a place where el Sayed might have said something clear — something like, “OK, I disavow the Muslim Brotherhood” — or moved on to play games. He moved on to play games. “Have you disavowed them?” he asked Teepell. “I haven’t heard you disavow them yet.”

Teepell played along. “I disavow them,” he said. “Do you? Great,” said el Sayed. “But here’s the thing about it. You’re asking the question because implicitly you assume that I’ll have dual loyalties, right? You assume that somehow I wouldn’t disavow, or that I’ll have some higher order allegiance than to the Constitution. Correct? Tommy, is that what you imply? Why would you think that about me?”

With that el Sayed had turned the question away from himself — did he disavow the Muslim Brotherhood? — and onto the previously unknown audience member Thomas Teepell. It appears that el Sayed considered his quick “Sure, yeah, absolutely, but I want to ask to the question that you’re asking” as a clear, ringing disavowal of the Muslim terrorist group. After that, he was just going after Teepell.

Teepell tried to keep his question on track, trying to repeat again that he had not heard el Sayed disavow the Muslim Brotherhood. And indeed, before the two were standing there in Caro, el Sayed had never before disavowed the Muslim Brotherhood. But there would be no more talk about that. El Sayed’s mission — and he seemed to have a supportive crowd in doing it — was to portray Teepell as Islamophobic.

El Sayed asked if Teepell had “asked everybody in your life” if they disavowed the Muslim Brotherhood. Teepell erred by taking el Sayed’s nonsense question seriously, answering, “I have not.” “So why are you asking me?” el Sayed said. “Because I have not heard you—” Teepell began, starting to repeat his original question. El Sayed stopped him. “No, no, no — answer the question, Tommy. Everybody knows the answer to it. Answer the question.”

The crowd began to make noise. Abdul was putting this Islamophobe in his place! El Sayed went on to lecture Teepell about how his question really concerned the Constitution and the meaning of the religion clauses of the First Amendment — as if any constitutional question was raised by a town hall attendee asking a candidate whether he disavowed the Muslim Brotherhood. El Sayed then went on to deliver a sermon about John F. Kennedy’s statements on Catholicism during the 1960 presidential campaign — as if there were any equivalence between the Catholic Church and a U.S. government-designated terrorist organization.

By the end, el Sayed had the crowd cheering and Tommy heading out the door. Just for the record, before el Sayed began his misdirection routine, when he asked Teepell why he asked the disavowal question, Teepell, had he been older and perhaps had some experience in confrontations, might have said something like: One, because one of your family members — your half sister — has said your family “has long been MB” and said that your mother, specifically, was involved with the Muslim Brotherhood. Two, you have been evasive in your answers to questions about your family’s relationship with the Muslim Brotherhood. Three, you attempt to attack and distract people who ask you the question. So given all that, just to remove any doubt, could you simply say the words, “I disavow the Muslim Brotherhood”?
That, of course, did not happen. Instead, el Sayed took another step forward in his campaign to portray valid questions about his background and his associations as Islamophobia.

articles.headline: Xbox biz guy deletes his X account less than 24 hours after saying game devs who don't embrace AI 'should not be in the business of being a business'
keyFacts: Xbox senior business strategy manager Brandon Stirrup deleted his X account after claiming developers who do not use AI should not be in business.
Stirrup stated that Xbox uses AI and encouraged others to adopt the technology for game development.
An Xbox source told PC Gamer that Stirrup deactivated his account due to the high volume of replies he received.
body: Xbox senior business strategy manager Brandon Stirrup is tired of pussyfooting around about AI: In a thread on X his week, he said that he wants the world to know that Xbox uses it, that he thinks everyone should be using it, and that he believes so strongly in the cause that he's willing to "take the hit" for saying so.
He has since deleted his X account. A source at Xbox tells PC Gamer that Stirrup opted to deactivate the account because of the volume of replies he was receiving.

Stirrup kicked off his thread on October 18 with a simple message saying he'd "vibe coded a bad but improvable game" over two days, although he only "actively" worked on it for about three hours. "I’m telling you I tried it and it’s true…anyone can build a game."
After saying that developers and studios who aren't incorporating AI into their strategies are "planning for a fake future," Stirrup went all in.

"Look if I'm fired tomorrow it will be because I told you the truth that nobody wants you to know. You can make a game with a simple prompt and yes you can make custom, tailored games. Everything you want in a game is right there for the taking, for better or worse," he wrote.
"I'm happy to take the hit if it means hundreds at Xbox can stop pretending that they're not using AI. It's time to accept and move forward."

After calling out the game industry and gamers alike for their reluctance to accept "reality," Stirrup stated explicitly that Xbox is "using AI" and then added, "My goal is to get this over with so we can move on as a company, despite the fact that some will persecute me for this: we use AI, just as all companies do in 2026."
Keep up to date with the most important stories and the best deals, as picked by the PC Gamer team.

There's a growing push for people to simply accept the "reality" of AI: Epic Games CEO Tim Sweeney, for instance, recently said the studio was "moving developers around to retool for maximum AI acceleration," after which the Epic Games Store ignited a firestorm by saying it "vibe coded" its new launcher. Xbox, now under the leadership of a former AI executive, recently launched a new Xbox Labs program to pursue emerging technologies, which naturally includes AI; even Linux recently dropped its rule requiring AI usage disclosures.
Stirrup himself is an enthusiastic AI evangelist: Last month, he also counselled laid-off employees to use Copilot to catalog their skills and accomplishments at the company.

Andy has been gaming on PCs from the very beginning, starting as a youngster with text adventures and primitive action games on a cassette-based TRS80. From there he graduated to the glory days of Sierra Online adventures and Microprose sims, ran a local BBS, learned how to build PCs, and developed a longstanding love of RPGs, immersive sims, and shooters. He began writing videogame news in 2007 for The Escapist and somehow managed to avoid getting fired until 2014, when he joined the storied ranks of PC Gamer. He covers all aspects of the industry, from new game announcements and patch notes to legal disputes, Twitch beefs, esports, and Henry Cavill. Lots of Henry Cavill.

body: Meta, the owner of Instagram, apologized for disabling an Instagram account run by No Kings Coalition, the organizers of the No Kings Day political rallies held across the country on Oct. 17.

Meta’s vice president of communications, Andy Stone, posted about the events on X the day of the rallies, with a follow-up message the next day. Stone said the blackout lasted about an hour in the middle of the protests and was an accidental shutdown caused by the engineering team’s automated systems detecting a traffic spike.
Specifically, the team detected a Claude AI tool reading profiles, posts and hashtags at an unusually high rate.
More from CNET
“It unfortunately took additional time for us to straighten out the situation with admin access to the IG account,” Stone wrote.
A representative for Meta did not immediately respond to a request for further comment.
The timing and duration of the outage were criticized by the No Kings Coalition, which wrote about it on the restored account.

“Even after visibility was restored, we still had no access to the account for hours,” the post read. “Meta still owes us an explanation. Restricting communications about voting in the middle of an election is unacceptable.”
As of Monday afternoon, the Instagram post had more than 70,000 likes. A representative for the No Kings Coalition did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

Saturday’s rallies took place a year after the group’s 2025 events, when protests were organized in 2,500 cities. The rallies, which began in June of last year, protest the policies of President Donald Trump. This year, the impending Nov. 3 midterm elections have added urgency to the events, with demonstrations focused on educating voters about early voting and expanding voter registration.

“The public is clearly primed to suspect that platforms’ high-profile content moderation decisions are politically motivated,” said Kate Ruane, director of the Free Expression Project at the nonprofit Center for Democracy & Technology, in an email.

Ruane noted that the automated moderation tools Meta blamed for the removal of the account have “important limitations including poor performance when making context-dependent decisions, especially for real-time and fast-moving events,” she said. “Users deserve to know when their content and accounts are being taken down and why, regardless of moderation method.”

Activist Brittany Packnett Cunningham, who said she was at a No Kings Coalition event in Dallas over the weekend, accused Meta of disrupting other accounts in the past during other political activism events.

“You mean to tell me in the middle of that day, it just so happens that the No Kings account is down for almost two hours?” she said in an Instagram video response. “I’ve got questions, and somebody needs to have some answers.”

Meta is also dealing with blowback about a separate issue. The company backtracked on plans to change its contractual language for business customers in a way that would have allowed it to scrape information for AI training.

articles.headline: UEFA piles pressure on FIFA demanding more from Gianni Infantino in damning letter
keyFacts: UEFA sent a letter to FIFA demanding answers to 42 questions regarding President Gianni Infantino’s conduct and his relationship with Donald Trump.
The governing body requested a substantive written response and supporting documentation from FIFA by November 2.
Senior UEFA executives are currently searching for a candidate to challenge Infantino in the next election, with a nomination deadline of November 18.
body: UEFA has sent FIFA a letter demanding answers to 42 questions surrounding Gianni Infantino’s presidency, including his relationship with Donald Trump.
The letter, seen by talkSPORT, is addressed to General Secretary Mattias Grafstrom, and seeks answers by November 2.
Gianni Infantino has faced mounting scrutiny over his presidency in recent months Getty
It follows FIFA President Infantino telling FIFA Council members in a meeting in Zurich last Thursday to put their questions in writing.
UEFA is seeking further clarity on a number of concerns raised in the meeting, including Infantino’s relationship with US President Donald Trump .

The letter also questions how Folarin Balogun’s red card came to be suspended at the World Cup, which allowed him to play against Belgium despite being sent off in the round before against Bosnia-Herzegovina.
UEFA want details as to how the FIFA Peace Prize was founded, and given to Trump at the 2026 World Cup draw in Washington DC.
Among their other grievances, European football’s governing body ask for more transparency FIFA Forward Enterprise (FFE), the failed plan to part-privatise FIFA .
UEFA’s letter to FIFA
“We formally request a substantive written response to each question, together with all supporting documentation by Monday, November 2,” the UEFA letter reads.
“Any refusal to disclose information or documents should be justified individually, with a clear explanation of the specific grounds relied upon.

“These questions require answers now. They cannot be deferred until the next meeting of the FIFA Council — nor can future governance reforms substitute for scrutiny of decisions already taken and accountability for them.”
Senior UEFA executives are still spearheading a move to find a candidate to run against Infantino at the next election.
The deadline to put forward a name is November 18.
Aleksander Ceferin heads up UEFA, who have long questioned Infantino’s suitability for his role as FIFA president Getty
Infantino has vowed to fight on, but there remain several unanswered questions despite the FIFA President apologising for FFE in Zurich last week.

UEFA President Aleksander Ceferin and his CONCACAF counterpart Victor Montagliani have both called for Infantino to resign, as has UEFA vice-president Laura McAllister and English FA chair Debbie Hewitt.
Among the major issues over which UEFA are seeking answers are the origins of FFE, where Infantino planned to sell off stakes in the world football governing body’s competitions to private investors
FIFA are asked by UEFA, “When was the idea of FFE first explored, by whom and with what objective?”

FIFA are also tasked with explaining why Josh Kushner’s Thrive Capital were granted exclusivity as an investor without consultation. Kusher is the younger brother of Jared Kushner, the son-in-law of U.S. president Donald Trump.
UEFA also ask whether Infantino had a financial interest in FFE.
infantino’s decisions throughout the summer have put him under serious pressure to keep his job AFP

The letter goes on to demand further information on “a series of decisions, transactions and interventions involving the FIFA President, the President of the United States [Trump] and individuals associated with him”.
These are outlined in detail as follows:
UEFA's question on Infantino-Trump dealings
” • The FIFA Peace Prize, which was not submitted to the FIFA Council for approval;
– The reported seven-year, approximately USD 4 million lease of office premises in Trump Tower, New York, involving Eric Trump, for premises reportedly unused for much of the year;
– The proposed agreement with Thrive Capital, led by Mr Joshua Kushner, a member of the US President’s family;
– The US President’s telephone call to the FIFA President requesting intervention in the Balogun disciplinary case;
– Reported advanced discussions involving the US President and individuals associated with him concerning a FIFA cryptocurrency;

– The World Cup sponsorship arrangement with Kalshi, a company reportedly advised and partly owned by Donald Trump Jr., including reports that Kalshi received extensive advertising exposure without providing financial consideration to FIFA;
– The last-minute relocation of the World Cup draw, reportedly at significant additional cost to FIFA, to the JFK/Donald Trump Center in Washington, D.C., instead of Las Vegas;
– The involvement of the US President’s daughter and grandson in the Club World Cup draw;

– The announcement of a USD 75 million investment in Palestine during the US President’s Board of Peace meeting, apparently without prior information being provided to, or approval sought from, the FIFA Finance Committee or Council;

– Public statements by White House representatives, including Andrew Giuliani and the US President himself, defending the FIFA President, supporting his continued presidency and criticising those questioning his leadership.”
UEFA want all documents relating to Balogun’s red card against Bosnia in the World Cup round of 32 to be shared.
The US striker saw his automatic one-game ban suspended following a call from President Trump to Infantino to review the matter, as talkSPORT exclusively revealed.
Infantino has always claimed he had no involvement in the decision to suspend Balogun’s red stressing FIFA’s disciplinary committee, which is independent, took the call.
The lack of clarity as to why the decision was made has led Infantino’s critics to question whether Infantino directly influenced the decision despite his denial.
And there are questions about Infantino’s use of a private jet, and the hosting of celebrities at World Cup final, and whether any FIFA costs were incurred in doing so.

articles.headline: How To Get Minior In Pokemon Go
keyFacts: The Pokemon Minior will debut in Pokemon Go on October 19.
Minior only spawns in the wild during real-world meteor showers between 5 PM and 11:59 PM local time.
Players must participate in multiple scheduled meteor shower events to collect all seven different Minior core colors.
body: A new Pokemon is landing soon in Pokemon Go . The meteorite Minior is making their debut in the mobile game beginning October 19, but you won't encounter them like a typical Pokemon.

Rather than periodically spawning in the wild, Minior's appearance is fittingly tied to meteor showers. The celestial Pokemon will only spawn on certain evenings when a real-world meteor shower is taking place, so you'll need to fire up the game on specific nights if you want to catch a glimpse of the new monster.

To help you add the falling star to your collection, here are some tips on how to catch Minior, including a schedule of upcoming meteor showers, how to change Minior's form, and whether the meteorite Pokemon can be shiny.

How To Get Minior
Minior Shower Schedule
How To Change Minior's Form
Can Minior Be Shiny?
How To Get Minior
Minior is a little different from other common Pokemon in that they won't just randomly spawn in the wild; you'll only have a chance to encounter one on evenings when a meteor shower is taking place.

During these specific nights, Minior will spawn on the map between 5 PM and 11:59 PM local time. From there, it's simply a matter of waiting for one to appear, then tapping on them to initiate a catch encounter. You can increase your odds of successfully catching the Pokemon by first feeding them a Razz Berry.

According to the official Pokemon Go website , a different Minior core color will debut during each of the aforementioned events, so you'll need to play the game during every meteor shower if you're hoping to add all seven core colors to your collection.

A couple of bonuses will also be available during the meteor shower events. You'll receive extra Stardust for catching Minior, and you'll see shooting stars streaking across the in-game sky from 5-9 PM local time. The game will also offer a free Timed Research that rewards you with a Star Piece and additional Stardust when completed.
How To Change Minior's Form
Minior doesn't evolve into any other Pokemon, but the meteorite Pokemon does come in several different variants.

Every Minior you encounter will initially be in Meteor Form, with the same brown outer shell. Once the Pokemon sustains enough damage during battle and their HP drops below 50 percent, their shell will break to reveal a different colored core.
There are seven core colors in total, one for every hue of the rainbow: red, orange, yellow, green, blue, indigo, and violet. One core color will debut during each meteor shower.
Can Minior Be Shiny?

At the moment, shiny Minior is not yet available in Pokemon Go. Shiny variants are typically introduced several months after a Pokemon first makes their debut, so shiny Minior may arrive down the line as part of some future event. However, nothing has been announced yet.

We're coming up on the end of October, but Pokemon Go still has a few events lined up for this month, including its annual Halloween celebration. You can see everything going on in the mobile game over the next few days in our October events roundup .

articles.headline: Trump predicts Paris is going to be a ‘Muslim City very soon’ as riots, looting rage in France
keyFacts: Around 500,000 people protested across France on Saturday, with smaller groups looting up to 2,000 stores and attacking police.
Donald Trump urged French President Emmanuel Macron to close borders and deport immigrants, predicting Paris will soon become a Muslim city.
French presidential candidate Marine Le Pen stated that Islam is compatible with the Republic ahead of the surge in violence.
body: Trump urged French President Emmanuel Macron to reduce migration into the country and “take those bad people out” — in apparent reference to his own mass-deportation campaign in the US.

“I told him a long time ago, ‘You’re making a big mistake in France. You’re letting everybody from the world come in. The whole world was coming in,'” Trump told reporters as he departed the White House for a campaign rally in Kansas.
“As you know, Paris is going to be a Muslim city very soon, and that wasn’t the deal. That wasn’t the deal. I told Emmanuel, ‘You should close up your borders.'”
Trump said he’s urged Macron to end mass migration into France for years, saying, “His borders are a problem.”
Trump made the remark about Paris when a reporter asked about Macron blaming his nation’s discontent on the US leader’s war with Iran, which increased global fuel costs.

“If Europe doesn’t close its borders and bring the criminals out, like the people that are protesting, Europe is finished. Europe has to close its borders, like I’ve been telling them for 10 years,” Trump added.
“They have to close their borders and they have to take people that hate their countries out because otherwise they’re finished. They will not have a chance of survival,” he went on.

Mass protests began in France last month over school conditions and have broadened to focus on the cost of living and inflation. On Saturday, about 500,000 people protested across France before smaller groups looted as many as 2,000 stores, attacked police and started fires across the country.
Footage showed looters and rioters from various racial and ethnic groups.
About 10% of France is Muslim, with a slightly higher percentage in Paris. Most are immigrants from or descendants of people from formerly French-ruled parts of Africa and the Middle East.

Trump said France needs to take out immigrants who “hate the country — They hate the buildings. They hate the people. They hate the art. They have to close their borders and they have to take those bad people out.”

Marine Le Pen, the populist conservative presidential candidate in France’s April election, has tempered criticism of Muslims as a whole, writing on X Thursday, ahead of the surge in violence, that “Islam is compatible with the Republic; I’ve said it ten times.”
Trump on Oct. 6 said that the mounting protests were about “Islam wanting to take over a once great Country.”

articles.headline: Grocery giant Ahold Delhaize confirms cyberattack forced US and European systems offline
keyFacts: Ahold Delhaize proactively took IT systems offline across its US and European brands following a cyberattack.
The company stated that physical stores remain open and there is currently no evidence that sensitive customer or employee data was stolen.
Ahold Delhaize is working to restore e-commerce services and has reported the incident to Dutch authorities.
body: Dutch grocery giant Ahold Delhaize, which operates US supermarket chains Food Lion, Giant Food, and Stop & Shop, said it proactively took IT systems offline following a cyberattack, affecting most of its US and European brands. The multinational chain originally disclosed the incident on October 12. “Ahold Delhaize is experiencing a security issue within its network,” it said at the time, adding that security teams, working to mitigate the issues, took “some” IT systems offline. On Monday, the company confirmed that it proactively took certain IT systems, including websites and apps, offline, affecting most of its brands, and said that “malicious actions of others” caused the security issue. “Taking systems offline to help protect them was a precautionary measure that affected most of our brands across Europe and the United States,” Frans Muller, president and CEO of Ahold Delhaize, said in a Monday statement. “The investigation to date confirms this was the right decision.” At this time, all of the physical stores remain open, and the investigation hasn’t uncovered any evidence to suggest the miscreants stole any “sensitive customer, associate, or partner data,” the disclosure said. The company last week notified the Dutch National Cyber Security Centre about the digital intruders, and on Monday filed a report with the Dutch police, according to the statement. Albert Heijn’s website and app are back online, and the company expects home deliveries to resume on Friday. Belgian e-commerce is fully operational, and e-commerce services at Ahold Delhaize’s American brands (Food Lion, Giant Food, Martin’s, Hannaford, and Stop & Shop) are expected to work “in the coming days.” The Etos and Gall & Gall websites are also up and running, along with the “majority of websites and apps” across brands serving central and southeastern Europe. Ahold Delhaize did not immediately respond to The Register’s questions about the cyberattack, including whether it was linked to attacks on refrigeration controllers at hundreds of French supermarkets beginning October 11. The attacks reportedly pushed temperatures as high as 122°F (50°C), spoiling food and causing fires at some locations. This latest cyberattack is Ahold Delhaize’s second in two years. A November 2024 digital break-in disrupted brands across the organization, with some Stop & Shop stores struggling to fill prescriptions, while Food Lion employees reported delayed and missing deliveries. INC Ransom claimed responsibility for the attack at the time and leaked some documents reportedly taken from the retailer's systems. Ahold Delhaize ultimately determined more than 2.2 million people’s data - including personal, financial, and health details - had been compromised. ®

articles.headline: Trump renews push to rename New Mexico ‘New America,’ touts higher home values and incomes
keyFacts: President Donald Trump renewed his push for New Mexico to change its name to 'New America,' claiming it would boost home values.
New Mexico Governor Michelle Lujan Grisham rejected the idea, stating the state's name is not up for debate.
Trump's post provided no formal process for the name change, which is expressly written into New Mexico's constitution.
body: President Donald Trump is giving New Mexico another branding pitch, urging the state to swap "Mexico" for "America" and suggesting the change could boost everything from home values to state pride.
"New Mexico should immediately change its name to New America. We are not Mexico, we are the United States of America!" Trump wrote on Truth Social.
"The name would add great value and prestige to the State! Home Values and Incomes would rise, and you would be even prouder while saluting our beautiful American Flag!"
The president also worked in a swipe at the state’s elections.
AFTER 'LAKE AMERICA,' TRUMP SUGGESTS A NEW NAME FOR THE STATE OF NEW MEXICO
"Maybe even the Crooked Elections, that New Mexico is known for, would become honest again!" he wrote.
MAP IT: DOJ ILLEGAL VOTING CRACKDOWN SWEEPS 17 STATES AS RAZOR-THIN ELECTIONS FACE SCRUTINY
Trump offered no evidence in the post to support his election allegation or explain how a name change would increase property values and incomes.

The suggestion revives an idea Trump floated last month, when he shared a map showing "Mexico" crossed out in red and replaced with "America." The White House amplified that post on its official X account.
TRUMP TAUNTS CANADA ON RENAMING LAKE ONTARIO THE 'LAKE AMERICA' AMID RISING BORDER TRADE RIFT
Trump also pitched the change during remarks at the RNC Midterm Convention on Sept. 9, suggesting neighboring New Mexico become "New America" and claiming the idea was popular.
"You have a neighboring state, New Mexico. We think it should be called New America," Trump said. "I’ll tell you, the people love the idea."
"I don’t know about the radical left. I’m sure it doesn’t like it, but the people love it," he added.

New Mexico’s Democratic governor, Michelle Lujan Grisham, pushed back at the time, telling Fox News Digital that the state’s name "isn’t up for debate — it’s been ours since before the United States existed."
She accused the White House of focusing on a distraction while her administration worked on child care, education, health care and housing.
NEW YORK GOV HOCHUL REJECTS TRUMP'S 'LAKE AMERICA' RENAMING WITH BLUNT MESSAGE
"While the White House wastes time coloring on maps, Nuevo México is busy doing the work," Lujan Grisham said last month.

Trump’s latest post calls for the state to change its name but does not lay out a formal process for doing so. New Mexico’s name is expressly written into Article I of its constitution, which states, "The name of this state is New Mexico."
HOUSE DEM DEBBIE DINGELL PLACES TRUMP'S LAKE ONTARIO NAME CHANGE IN THE CROSSHAIRS
The proposal follows Trump’s moves to rename Lake Ontario "Lake America" for federal use and the Gulf of Mexico the "Gulf of America."
Fox News Digital's Amanda Macias contributed to this report.

articles.headline: Amazon is taking its biggest shot at Nvidia yet with new TorchNeuron dev tool
keyFacts: Amazon Web Services released TorchNeuron to allow AI startups to run PyTorch applications on Amazon's Trainium chips without rewriting code.
Amazon claims this tool simplifies migration to its cloud infrastructure and offers better price-performance for training and inference than Nvidia-based providers.
Amazon plans to contribute code to the PyTorch project to make the framework less dependent on Nvidia hardware.
body: On Monday, Amazon Web Services released a tool called TorchNeuron that lets AI startups easily move their AI apps onto Amazon’s AI chip, Trainium. In doing so, Amazon is also taking a direct stab at the the software advantage that has helped Nvidia become the default hardware choice for AI apps, and spurred its rise as AI hardware provider of choice.

TorchNeuron works with PyTorch, a free, open-source toolkit that developers use to build, train, and run AI models. It lets AI apps written with PyTorch run on Trainium by changing just one line of configuration, according to Amazon — no code rewrite required.

Amazon says about 85% of AI apps are written with PyTorch. Facebook originally developed it, but since 2022, it has been part of the Linux Foundation, which maintains open-source projects. Nvidia has spent years ensuring its CUDA software — the software infrastructure that allows apps to run on Nvidia GPUs and its other hardware — seamlessly supports AI apps written with PyTorch. As a result, Nvidia’s hardware is now deeply embedded in the toolkit, essentially by default.

TorchNeuron is adapted from PyTorch, so developers who know PyTorch already know how to use it. Amazon isn’t the first company to attempt to easily bring their chips to the platform. PyTorch users can also port their apps to AMD GPUs or even Apple’s chips with a simple configuration change.

However, Amazon argues that porting to Trainium isn’t just easy; it also gives AI startups access to Amazon’s entire cloud. Unsurprisingly, AWS claims that this is a better choice for startups than using neoclouds, many of which are tied to Nvidia and its hardware, like Coreweave, Nebius, and Firmus.

“You’re building on AWS. You’re not betting on a single-purpose compute provider and scrambling to build everything else around it,” Colin Brace, VP of Technology Software at AWS Annapurna Labs (the unit that makes Amazon’s custom chips) told TechCrunch via email. “On AWS,” he continued, “the infrastructure to go from prototype to production is already there, allowing a founder to move fast and scale when they need to.”

AWS says that because the same chip both handles training (teaching the AI model) and inference (putting the finished model to work, as when it answers a user’s question), and is tightly integrated with the cloud infrastructure that startups need, its cloud will save them money, even if AWS doesn’t offer the cheapest per-token price.

“Trainium’s value is price-performance plus the fact that it’s one platform for both training and inference, which improves the economics across a full workload,” Brace said. “Look at Deepgram — they moved to Trainium using native PyTorch, support and they’re processing 70% more audio per dollar at production-grade accuracy.” Deepgram is an AI voice app provider, a competitor to ElevenLabs.
But Amazon isn’t content to just give PyTorch app developers an easy option to move to its cloud.

Amazon also says it is pushing PyTorch to be less automatically centered on Nvidia, and it will contribute the code to do that to the main PyTorch project. In the blog post announcing the new tool, the company wrote:

“Amazon’s approach extends beyond its own hardware. The company is contributing changes upstream to PyTorch itself, working with the PyTorch community to remove code that ties the framework to specific chips. The goal is to make PyTorch more hardware-agnostic for the entire developer community, not just Trainium users.”

While such a tactic is undoubtedly good for those who are selling hardware and cloud services that compete with Nvidia, one of the points of PyTorch is to hide all the pesky difficulties of getting AI code to run on hardware. We’ll have to wait and see if pushing Nvidia out that far gives developers more choice and more affordable options, as Amazon promises, or just more configuration headaches.

Either way, if Amazon succeeds in deeply uncoupling PyTorch from Nvidia, this could have much bigger ramifications for the GPU giant than simply dealing with chip competitors. As Brace said: “The real story is removing the lock-in that kept developers from having a real choice at all.”

articles.headline: Moonlighter dev delays Steam playtest for its "Tower Defensevania" ReVamp over concerns that AI copycats might clone it before launch
keyFacts: Developer Digital Sun delayed the Steam playtest for its game ReVamp due to concerns about AI-powered cloning.
The studio will now host a smaller, contained playtest on Discord starting October 29th to mitigate risks.
Digital Sun plans to open a public playtest for ReVamp around January before the game's full launch in March 2027.
body: Digital Sun - the indie studio behind moreish roguelike Moonlighter and moody RTS Cataclismo - has delayed a planned Steam playtest for its next game, ReVamp, citing concerns over "games being reverse-engineered, cloned and published before the original is even out."

The developer was planning to let folks into its vampiric "Tower Defensevania" ReVamp near the end of this spooky month, but a new trend of gen-AI copycats cloning both old and unreleased games left the studio worried.

"So many of you signed up for ReVamp's first playtest here on Steam (thank you!), but we've decided to start with something more contained on our Discord, with the public playtest coming a bit later," the developer wrote in a recent Steam blog post.

Digital Sun pointed the finger at "news of games being reverse-engineered, cloned and published before the original is even out," and worried that "sharing a build with tens of thousands of players" months prior to its full launch is "too big a risk."

From here, Digital Sun will grant access to ReVamp's first playtest in waves starting from the 29th of October, via Discord. "Even if you don't get in right away, we'd love for you to join the conversation around ReVamp as we let more players in. We hope to open the public playtest around January. To everyone who requested access here on Steam: we're sorry for the change of plans, and thank you for your patience," the studio added.
ReVamp launches in full on 25th March, 2027. Here's hoping the move can successfully shoo away any would-be clones.
Digital Sun isn't the only developer having to work around the gen-AI boom. Xbox recently announced an entire department that sounds like it's focused on gen-AI game-making, as just one example.

Meanwhile, Alliance Arts outright cancelled a Steam Next Fest demo for its anime-inspired Russian Roulette game, Drunken Goddess Reflux, because of similar issues. "We are concerned that, based on the content of the demo, works imitating or replicating this game's presentation and gameplay could be quickly produced using AI or other tools and released ahead of the game's launch," the company said last week.

Steam Next Fest 2026 should be a great occasion to discover new and exciting games that were previously nowhere near your radar. However, as we reported earlier today, the shadow of generative AI looms over the entire event and could dampen an otherwise great Steam tradition.

articles.headline: Japanese Tekken Players are Likening Tekken 6’s Rollback Netcode Mod to Serious Crimes and the Fighting Game Community is Split
keyFacts: A community member created a mod for Tekken 6 that adds rollback netcode, allowing users to play the game online.
Japanese and Korean players have criticized the mod as copyright infringement, while many Western players defend the project as a way to play older games.
Bandai Namco has not yet taken action against the mod, which remains available to the public.
body: Two weeks ago, a Tekken player created a mod that allowed users to play the game online with rollback netcode, sparking a community-wide debate between Western players and competitors based in Japan and Korea.

The mod, made by a community member named Ekspym, became an instant hit among Tekken players, reaching more than 10,000 players as of October 17 and a recorded 4,547 downloads as of October 15. According to the mod’s readme, “the package contains neither the PS3 firmware nor the game,” though it acts essentially like an emulator.

It sparked a viral conversation regarding the current state of Tekken 8 (with many players seeming to prefer Tekken 6 out of the two games), but perhaps more surprisingly, received massive pushback from players in Japan and Korea.

One of the loudest voices speaking out against this mod was celebrated fighting game pro Dogura. “The pirated version of Tekken 6? That thing crosses the line way too much, and I'm horrified that no one overseas is raising negative voices about it,” he wrote in a post on Twitter/X. “When our fundamental values and sense of morality differ this much, we probably can't even have a conversation. I'm praying that the right response is taken.”

Another Japanese user named Higemura also had a viral take on the situation, worrying that the Tekken series might end due to mods such as this one. “It seems like you're running the Tekken 6 service without permission, but the people doing it should really think about what they're actually up to. If the population flows over there and money stops going to the official service, the Tekken series will come to an end, right?” they wrote.

“I totally get having an attachment to Tekken 6, since I love the bound system and move balance too, but if that's the case, you should develop a new fighting game that's Tekken 6-like. The way things are going now, you're just infringing on rights and gobbling up Bandai Namco's assets and potential customers without permission.”

Overall, it seems that Japanese players take copyright very seriously and consider such mods to be outright theft. This attitude is also reflected from some players based in Korea, with one Korean user likening it to sexual assault. (Another Japanese player even compared it to necrophilia, while another made a baffling comparison to the Civil Rights Movement.)

This, of course, prompted a massive discussion that has taken hold of the broader fighting game community. The attitudes toward such mods are far more lenient among Western players, with one writing, “Please tell me how I am supposed to ‘properly’ support the game when I cannot even buy it here? If I take a broken old bike out of the trash and repair it, why are you saying I am stealing from the bike corporation? It was trash. There was no way to buy it!”
“Explain why it is more morally righteous to demand people to pay for used copies of an old game on the secondhand market that the developers won't see any money from,” another said.

Ekspym’s Tekken 6 mod is still alive and well, and has not yet received any pushback from Bandai Namco — though it has, inadvertently, exposed a very intriguing difference in opinions about emulation and modding between Western fighting game players and those based in East Asia.

(It is worth noting, though, that some Japanese players are pushing back against this mindset, with one even pointing out a pro player using a cracked arcade cabinet in response to Dogura's initial tweet.)
This is the latest Tekken-related news to go viral after Baki’s Yujiro Hanma was finally shown off at Evo France, and he’s just as terrifying as we expected him to be.

articles.headline: We all want to offload our most tedious tasks. But what do we lose in the process?
keyFacts: Companies including Meta and OpenAI have launched personal AI agents to automate everyday administrative tasks for consumers.
Meta's Muse became the market leader with over eight million downloads in its first month, according to an estimate.
Personal AI agents require extensive private data access and can commit unpredictable errors, according to experts and users.
body: If there’s one thing a busy person doesn’t need, it’s more information. More emails, more notifications, more infinite feeds — the steady drip of data spells doom for the overstimulated American. And if you’re a busy parent, like me, sometimes it feels like a flood: school emails, doctor’s appointments, so many little things to buy.

Even things that used to be simple are harder. I recently listed an item on Facebook Marketplace, which quickly meant I was replying to offers and getting ghosted for the better part of a weekend before finding someone who, after a detailed back-and-forth about the most likely place to find a parking spot in my neighborhood, finally took my old baby swing away.

If only I’d had Muse. You’ve probably seen the ads on Instagram promising “AI that gets it done for you.” The new personal AI agent app from Meta can not only automate your Facebook Marketplace tasks, but also sort your emails, manage your calendar, and buy your groceries. And it’s free — unless you’re using it most of the day or you want access to Meta’s most powerful models , at which point it costs $20 or $100 a month. It all sounds, in a word, magical.

Muse is probably the personal AI agent you’ve heard of — and it’s currently the market leader with more than 8 million downloads in its first month, according to one estimate — but there’s now a small army of these bots: OpenAI recently announced Dots , X has Grok Bot , and there’s Instinct , which is currently invite-only and operates entirely in iMessage or WhatsApp. They all offer the same promise: to remove friction from your busy life.

For the last two weeks, I’ve been handing over more and more of my life to AI agents in pursuit of making my life a little simpler. What I found is that AI is unpredictable, and so are AI agents. When I first began using Muse, it started doing things I didn’t ask it to do. It offered to help with random email threads and created dossiers on people in my work meetings. It generated a detailed report on nearby apple-picking destinations based on a calendar invite from my wife. To me, an AI agent doing these things without prompting isn’t helpful. It’s unnerving.
But ultimately, I came away believing that AI agents can make your life easier.

That might mean giving an AI agent more access than you’re comfortable with — handing over lots of login credentials and possibly even your credit card. The more you rely on an AI agent, the more you risk outsourcing your decision-making. This raises real questions about how much agency we want to hold onto in our lives — even the tedious parts.
The leap of faith
Let’s get one thing out of the way first: To make an agent work for you, you’ll have to sacrifice a tremendous amount of privacy and grant it permission to access a lot of personal information.

Muse and its competitors can do the classic generative AI tricks, like draft emails or make you a fitness plan. If you’d like the agent to send one of those emails, however, you’ll have to grant it permission to access pretty much everything in your Gmail account. If you want it to schedule workouts, it will need access to your calendar. If you want the agent to buy anything on your behalf, it will need your credit card. If you want it to book your doctor’s appointments, it will need the credentials to log into your healthcare portal. The more permission you grant it, the more the agent can do for you, but that also opens up more opportunities for the agent to misunderstand you or your instructions (more on this in a moment).

This process of sharing your digital life with an AI agent means you’re giving an untold amount of personal information to tech companies, who don’t always behave ethically , and who sell user data for profit . For now, Meta says that it does not share Muse data or conversations with its ad systems, although privacy experts warn that doesn’t really matter since those systems monitor what Muse does on your behalf. Nevertheless, Muse’s early days were filled with security and privacy blunders .

But without all of this info and access, the AI agents aren’t very useful. So if you’re not comfortable letting a bot into all of your accounts, an AI agent is probably never going to be the solution to your digital administrative exhaustion. But even if you are willing to hand that over, there are still other barriers to an agent’s efficiency and effectiveness.
The blank slate problem

AI agents, like a lot of new software tools (including chatbots), suffer from the blank slate problem . The blank slate problem essentially means that people don’t know how to get started. This might be because you don’t know about the tool’s capabilities, or because you simply don’t know what would be helpful. There might be some trust issues, too.

As with AI in general, we don’t exactly know how AI agents work. That means we don’t know exactly what they can do or how they’ll do it, according to Pattie Maes , a professor of media technology at MIT — so it’s necessary to do a lot of babysitting. “I feel like I’m not gaining a lot of time because I can’t completely trust the system,” Maes told me about her experience with Muse, “and I can’t predict how it will behave and what it will do.”

Some advice I heard from early adopters of these tools, however, is to start small. “In the beginning, it’s very hard to trust that it’s going to just magically do a really big thing,” Julie Zhuo , founder of the AI company Sundial and an early Facebook employee, told me about her experience using personal agents. “So you give it smaller tasks, and once you see it succeed, then I feel like you develop more trust that it can tackle bigger things.”

This is surely why Meta decided that Muse needed an Ideas tab full of small tasks the AI agent can do. Muse will also send you a lot of push notifications to prompt you to do stuff, like reply to specific emails or prepare for a meeting. That detailed report on apple-picking destinations? That was a notification about something I didn’t ask Muse to do. Muse also sent me a notification about a show hosted by a podcast I don’t listen to and another one with details about a Halloween party I wasn’t invited to, as well as several evening digests that included lists of things it had already bugged me about that day. Notifications are either helpful nudges or time-consuming attention thieves, depending on your worldview. However, if you fall into the latter category and turn off the notifications from your always-on personal agent, you’re inevitably forfeiting some friction reduction opportunities.
This gets to the heart of one of the big questions I have about AI agents: How helpful are they, really, if it’s this difficult to know what to do with them?

These agents worked much better when I drove the conversation. While wondering what to do with my new agents, literally staring at the blank slate, cost me some time, I found myself thrilled at how easy basic productivity tasks became. Adding events to my calendar, making to-do lists and then being held accountable for stuff not getting done, being reminded to reply to an email — it was these kinds of simple, administrative chores where I saw personal AI agents really start to save me time.

Other tech journalists seemed to have similar experiences. Eli Tan at the New York Times raved about Muse handling a call to his insurance company. Nicole Nguyen saved time by enlisting Dots for help canceling unwanted subscriptions. Allison Johnson at The Verge had Muse do a whole list of “pebble-in-your-shoe annoyances” she’d been putting off, and among other things, the agent succeeded in helping her buy an entire camping kitchen. Still, she wrote something that stuck with me: “the dirty secret of productivity hacks is that doing more stuff often doesn’t feel like things are being removed from your plate; somehow it just invites more tasks.”

This gets to the heart of one of the big questions I have about AI agents: How helpful are they, really, if it’s this difficult to know what to do with them? There’s a learning curve, sure, where succeeding at one thing gives you an idea to try something else and have some certainty about how well the AI agent will handle the task. But as the notifications roll in, and you spend more and more time texting with a piece of software, how much time are you really freeing up by using these tools? At a point, enlisting an agent with its own computer to do your chores still amounts to using one app to save yourself from using a different app.
The ironies of automation

Even when they have access to a lot of your information, and you’ve come up with some things for them to do, AI agents can be unpredictable. Because despite reading every email in your inbox or scanning every purchase on your latest bank statement, AI agents still can’t read your mind, and you can’t necessarily guess how they’ll interpret your commands. They can misunderstand you and, armed with the keys to your digital life, do some real damage.

Some people are already learning about the unpredictability of AI agents the hard way. One early adopter, Matt Robb, gave Muse the keys to his Facebook Marketplace account and was surprised when buyers started showing up at his front door ready to pick up their purchase. Muse, without asking Robb, had told them where to go. It turns out, without realizing it, Robb had given the agent permission to do so, and the agent had simply decided that the most efficient way to get buyers to Robb’s door was to give them his home address.

This dilemma is an example of a decades-old set of concepts known as the “ironies of automation.” Identified by psychologist Lisanne Bainbridge in a paper published in 1983 , the ironies of automation help explain why things go wrong when humans give a machine too much control. As Vera Liao , an electrical engineering and computer science professor at the University of Michigan who studies human–AI interaction, explained to me: More advanced automation leads to more consequential errors, and the more humans rely on automation, the worse we get at catching those errors. “Even in simple tasks like judging whether AI output is wrong, people consistently accept wrong AI outputs even if they could have gotten it right on their own,” Liao said.

In some cases, like the time Muse read a journalist’s private messages , things go wrong as a result of poorly designed software, but more often than not, it’s the fault of the user who gives instructions that are too vague, giving the agent space to get creative, which isn’t always a good thing.

I had my own misunderstanding with Instinct. In a text message, the agent reminded me about a couple of emails I’d received and prompted me to follow up. When I replied to the text, I asked Instinct to show me possible replies to these emails. The AI agent instead just sent the responses it wrote. I audibly gasped.
Looking back at our chat history, I could see why Instinct interpreted my instructions that way. I effectively gave the machine too much control and then failed to manage the automation properly.

Leaning on AI to do your thinking is an example of what psychologists call cognitive offloading, where you employ an external tool to reduce your effort to complete a task. It makes completing the task easier, sure, but you also open yourself to mistakes . In this case, an AI agent took my instructions too literally, and I failed to catch the error. I can only imagine how a small oversight could turn into a cascade of catastrophes that need cleaning up. All it takes is one poorly worded email sent to the wrong person, and you might have hours of explaining to do — all because you were trying to save yourself 30 seconds of writing.
The real world slop

While I was testing all these agents, I talked to a mix of experts and early adopters. Their opinions were decidedly split about whether these tools were useful out of the box, without a ton of oversight and training by the user. The experts, who had all studied AI in academic settings, all brought up the ironies of the automation problem, where AI makes errors that humans can’t catch. And Maes, the MIT professor, pointed at another consequence: By outsourcing so many tasks to agents, we’re actually creating more work for everyone, including the human service workers who have to interact with this technology instead of us.

“There’s just more and more slop,” Maes told me. “We risk, in a world where agents do all the tasks for us, becoming so dependent on them that the world also isn’t created for us to interact with anymore, but it’s only created for our agents to interact with others, with services.” (We’re already seeing versions of how dominant tech platforms can fundamentally reshape real-world spaces: Think of how Starbucks no longer looks like a coffee shop where you can hang out all day, and is instead built and staffed around mobile order pick-up.)

The early adopters were decidedly more optimistic. Matt Van Horn, an entrepreneur who co-founded the ridesharing service that became Lyft, has been tinkering with agents since the craze started late last year. He’s currently telling his friends and family to use Instinct, which he described to me as “the most ambitious and aggressive” AI agent.
“I’ve been pushy with my mom and my wife,” Van Horn told me, “and saying, ‘Hey, you should sign up for this. It’s magical.’”

“My wife does not care about living in the future, but we have four kids,” Van Horn continued. She recently took a picture of a parking ticket and sent it to Instinct, no description, no instructions. Instinct, which had her credit card, just paid the ticket.

At the same time, outsourcing certain chores to AI agents causes real-world problems. Some of these AI agents can make phone calls, for instance, which can lead to some confusion when a human is on the other end of the line. Van Horn told me about the unfortunate time he enlisted an AI agent to reserve a room at a karaoke bar. “The karaoke place said, ‘Are you an AI?’” Van Horn said. “‘I don’t want to talk to an AI. Please connect me to Matt, the person.’ And so Muse had failed to book that for me.” Van Horn, undeterred, found something called Fo, an AI agent that will bring in human help to complete a task. Fo succeeded at making the reservation, although the entire ordeal surely took longer than if Van Horn had picked up the phone himself and talked to the karaoke bar himself.

At best, the times these tools worked and actually saved me time were rather mundane. I made a doctor’s appointment online using Instinct. Zhuo, the early Facebook employee, planned a party for her college reunion — everything from tracking down everyone’s emails to sending out invitations via Paperless Post. But she’s also said these kinds of applications of agentic AI “ read more like vitamins than painkillers .” In the startup world, “vitamins” refers to a product that offers a vague benefit, and “painkillers” solve a big, immediate problem. If you’re a startup, you want to sell painkillers.

If you’re ready to give an agent a go, be prepared for the bot to make mistakes, and assume you won’t catch all of them. As Liao, the University of Michigan professor, put it, “Choose to use agents for tasks that you can tolerate the consequences of errors.”

In an effort not to create more emails or alerts or feeds to sift through, I’ve stopped using Muse. Like any new tool, it will get better and more useful as more people use it, so maybe I’ll revisit it in the future. I still have a text thread going with Instinct, however. It messages me from time to time, flagging an email or offering to help with an upcoming event. When there’s a clear payoff to giving the agent the go-ahead, I reply. Otherwise, I leave it on read.

articles.headline: Startup taps underwater volcano as energy source in "proof point" test
keyFacts: Endurance Energy successfully tested the world's first subsea geothermal power plant near an underwater volcano in the Pacific Ocean.
The prototype generated net-positive electricity for less than 10 seconds to demonstrate the technical feasibility of underwater geothermal energy.
The company must now prove that subsea geothermal power can operate consistently and remain cost-effective compared to land-based alternatives.
body: The world’s first demonstration of a subsea geothermal power plant has taken place near an active underwater volcano almost a mile below the ocean surface. It generated less than 10 seconds of net-positive electricity but showed the technical feasibility of tapping another form of renewable energy underwater.

The three-week test deployment of the 3-ton prototype power plant took place at the Axial Seamount in the northeast Pacific Ocean in September. Endurance Energy, the Seattle-based startup behind the effort, aims to eventually commercialize subsea geothermal power for Pacific island nations and other customers looking for alternatives to importing expensive fossil fuels.

“The deep ocean gives us unlimited cold seawater for cooling, and its weight keeps the system and the well pressurized, so our plants can be compact,” said Andrew Redd, founder and CEO of Endurance Energy, in an email to Ars.

But efforts to tap geothermal power on the seafloor face many different challenges from land-based geothermal projects, which can also add up to higher installation and operational costs. So Endurance Energy must demonstrate consistent underwater operations as well as prove the approach can be cost-effective.

“It’s probably technically feasible, but it would undoubtedly be more expensive than to do it on land,” said Roland Horne, professor of energy science & engineering at Stanford University, in an emailed response to Ars.
Deep sea drilling

Endurance Energy’s deployment required a subsea lander drill to deploy from the ship Ocean Guardian—operated by Stabbert Maritime—and drill two holes in the seafloor at a depth of about 5,000 feet (1,524 meters). That means the test took place at a depth exceeding 2.5 times the height of the One World Trade Center building in New York City, which is the tallest building in the United States.
