articles.headline: Here's how we would build out the perfect modular electric Slate truck
keyFacts: The Slate Truck is a modular electric vehicle that starts at $24,950 and allows buyers to customize it with over 200 different accessories.
Customizing the truck with various add-ons can significantly increase the final price, with some builds approaching $40,000 or more.
The base model has an estimated range of 205 miles, which limits the vehicle's suitability for long-distance travel.
body: Here's how we would build out the perfect modular electric Slate truck
Who wants a battery-powered 1970s throwback?

The Slate Truck is about as unique a vehicle as there is. The modular electric truck ships from the factory as a bare-bones two-seat pickup in a single (slate gray) color. But the fun begins when you trick it out with a catalog of over 200 add-ons. After hours of tinkering with the configurator, here's our ideal throwback build.

When customizing your Slate Truck, it helps to have a clear theme in mind. And what better theme than "1970s Ford Bronco"? Granted, no Bronco ever looked exactly like this. But if you concocted a blend of those old trucks and a modern EV, it might not be far off.

The catch? Once you add enough accessories to transform the Slate into something that fits your vision, the price may no longer be a selling point. While you can get the bare-bones version for $24,950, our build approaches $40,000 — and it will get even expensive after accounting for Slate's as-yet-unpriced accessories. The potential for upsell overspending is real, and you should know that going in.
The basics

Although it leaves the factory quite threadbare, the Slate Truck doesn't have to stay that way. You can turn it into a five-seat SUV (fastback or squareback) or a Jeep-like option that would pair well with an open-air back seat. We went with the squareback SUV, which brings the starting price up to $29,950 before accessories.

This includes a roll cage, extra airbags, a bench seat for three and the squared-off shell. That serves as a worthy foundation for our '70s-inspired build, since sleeker-looking fastback SUVs weren't around then. Plus, it's more practical for cargo and, even better, saves us $2,000.
Throwback style

While each Slate Truck starts as a muted gray, you can wrap it in a variety of colors. For our base, we went with the Michigan Copper full wrap ($670). This foundation evoked late '70s stylings more than other options.

After that, we added the Throwback body decal ($320) and Creamsicle shoulder decals ($190). This is what sells the nostalgic look, with the Atari-esque stripe running down the side. Slate also offers mirror and rocker accents, but the colors didn't fully match and risked overcrowding the side.
The front lamps, taillights and grille each get "Dots" plates. For under $160 total, they help the truck's face look a bit more era-appropriate.
Bronco on the outside

We also added an upgraded front bumper ($500) and rear bumper ($600), fog lights ($300), fender flares ($150), a spare tire carrier ($550) and running boards ($350). The bumpers and fog lights accentuate the squared-off look of old 4x4s, and the flares give it a wider, more aggressive appearance. Meanwhile, the running boards are a practical touch, making our lifted build easier to climb into.

That's thanks to the as-yet-unpriced lift kit, which reportedly adds about two inches of height. We paired that with all-terrain tires on 17-inch wheels ($1,100). Slate also sells 20-inch wheels, but the 17s' larger sidewalls, softer ride and more theme-appropriate look nudged things in their favor.

Although our build resembles something you could take off-road, a reality check is in order. This rear-wheel-drive truck is better suited to dirt roads and snowy driveways than steep trails or deep mud.
The roof rack completes the look

A boxy, '70s-style vehicle without a roof rack looks incomplete. So we added the squareback roof rack ($650) on Slate's T-rail ($125). The automaker also sells carriers for bikes, kayaks, skis and paddleboards that attach to it. There's even a roof basket for frequent campers.

Just keep in mind that Slate estimates just 205 miles of range for the base pickup, and our heavier SUV will likely be even worse. That doesn't lend itself to long road trips into the wilderness. We can only take our '70s Bronco cosplay so far.
Old and new on the inside

Lest you forget that you're riding in something nostalgic, the inside has similar references. The Throwback interior decal ($50)m Magma accents on the lower dash and climate knobs (both still unpriced) call back to the exterior side stripe, but without making the cabin too loud.

Everything else sticks with the stock dark interior. That includes added Slate Black armrests ($50 for the doors, with the console armrest's price still unannounced). On a more practical note, we threw in a center console ($250), door cubby organizers ($50) and all-weather floor liners for the front and back of the cabin ($135 total).

One thing we couldn't add: power windows. Although it's more Slate's choice than a nostalgic one, why not call it another ode to the past? Slate previously listed power windows but pulled them later, with a spokesperson saying they could eventually return.
A touch of tech
The Slate ships by default with no screen or stereo. The idea is to use your phone for both jobs, although add-ons can fill in some gaps.

That lack of built-in audio is one of the hardest limits for a music or podcast lover to get past. Fortunately, Slate gives you several accessory options, including a mount for Bluetooth speakers. We went with the center speaker ($250) plus a pair of front left and right speakers ($150). $400 seems like a reasonable enough price to pay for a modern sound system.
Then we added Slate's Bluetooth steering wheel controls (price TBD) to skip songs and answer calls without taking hands off the wheel. You can only pretend you're in the 1970s to a point.

Also in our build: the tablet mount (unpriced) alongside the standard phone mount. A larger screen for navigation was too hard to pass up. Although it isn't confirmed whether the mount can support it, we'd also look into one of those portable CarPlay / Android Auto displays to run car-specific apps.

We also added the Five Switch upgrade ($40) for a row of physical light switches. This accessory is required for the fog lights, which no wannabe Bronco should go without. We added the home charger ($479), which, according to Slate, lets you fully charge the truck in five to eight hours. The company has said it will also sell adapters for older public chargers, since the truck is designed for Tesla's plug.
What we skipped
There are plenty of other things you can do with the Slate, as long as you're willing to let its cost add up.

Besides the fastback body we mentioned, we also skipped the lowering kit. This gives the EV a street truck look, but it's not the best choice for our old-school theme. We passed on the animated front and rear lights ($850) for the same reason.

Slate's other upgrades include a roof light bar for $800 and LED taillights for $375. A light bar on a nostalgic wagon might conjure emergency response vehicle vibes, which... isn't what we're going for. There's also camping gear, like heavier-duty roof platforms ($700 to $1,230) and inflatable camp tables and chairs from Flated ($150 to $300). Those may come in handy, as long as the camping trek isn't too far out in the wilderness.
Slate also sells more interior colors, wraps from other licensed brands and a cellular bridge for tracking. None of those fit our needs.
The bill

The squareback SUV gives us a $29,950 starting point. Our accessories come out to about $6,518, although Slate hasn't announced prices for several of them. Especially with the unpriced lift kit, the final accessories tab could easily approach $8,000. The destination fee is $1,450.

Add it up, and we're looking at $37,918 — and that's without the lift kit and other "price TBD" accessories. Suddenly, the EV is less of a budget-friendly option and closer to what you'd expect to find on your local lots right now. And with a mere 205 miles of range, that's a purchase to think long and hard about before pulling the trigger.

Still, it's a highly specific truck that's entirely ours. We chose every piece of it, which isn't something you can say about most $40,000-ish vehicles. And perhaps more importantly, those who don't need any bells and whistles (or who are happy to add them later) can get a minimal build for under $25,000 before taxes and fees. It's a setup that's truly unique in the EV world, and one that might attract more than a few buyers.

articles.headline: US bans DeepSeek AI from government use as tech tension with China continues
keyFacts: The US Department of Homeland Security has banned the use of DeepSeek AI technology across most civilian government agencies.
The order prohibits the use of DeepSeek models and any technology built using them, though Department of Defense agencies are excluded.
The ban follows claims from US officials and firms that Chinese companies have engaged in the malicious exploitation and copying of American AI models.
body: - Published
The US has ordered all artificial intelligence (AI) technology from the Chinese firm DeepSeek to be removed from most government systems.
The Department of Homeland Security (DHS) has banned all use of DeepSeek within civilian government agencies, and any technology built with the aid of its AI models.
As a powerful AI model that is open source - meaning it is free to access and less expensive to use - DeepSeek has been seen as a disruptive force in the ongoing AI technology race.
While the DHS notice did not detail the exact security concerns surrounding DeepSeek, the White House has this year criticised AI firms from China.
The DHS, DeepSeek, and the Chinese embassy in Washington DC have been contacted for comment.
The DHS made the order public on Monday, but the ban took effect from the end of July.

The order is specific to civilian agencies, including the Department of the Treasury, the Department of State and the Department of Justice. However, agencies within the Department of Defense are excluded.
The ban follows criticism of Chinese AI from the Trump administration, and from American firms.
White House tech lead Michael Kratsios wrote earlier this year in an internal memo that "malicious exploitation" of American AI firms had been occurring, mainly by rival firms in China.

Anthropic and OpenAI, both of which are poised to list on the public stock market in the coming months, have also claimed to have had their AI models essentially copied by some Chinese AI firms, including DeepSeek.
US president Donald Trump has made clear that he sees China as the key US rival when it comes to development of AI, something he sees as crucial to the future of the country.
DeepSeek has grown in popularity since its initial public release in 2025, with models being in such demand that the company's servers have gone down at times.

While DeepSeek's free chatbot app is one of the most downloaded apps in the Apple App Store rankings, its AI models are also used by US tech companies. Companies like Snowflake, Vercel and OpenRouter all incorporate DeepSeek in their offerings to customers.
Startups have flocked to open source models like DeepSeek.
For a technology or AI developer, using DeepSeek in their work costs a fraction of what a closed model like Google's Google's Gemini, Anthropic's Claude or OpenAI's Codex would.
Similarly, the expense borne by DeepSeek to develop its models has been astronomically less than what it has cost US AI firms to develop their own.

Last year, DeepSeek said it took about $6m (Â£4.5m) to train the debut version of its model, while the costs associated with OpenAI's GPT-4 were roughly $100m. Such revelations sent tech stocks tumbling.

The most recent version of DeepSeek was released last week. Users of the model have praised it online, saying it beats even the most advanced AI tools out of OpenAI on common tasks for AI tools like computer software coding.

articles.headline: Dramatic images show violent unrest sweeping across France
keyFacts: Widespread violence and looting erupted across France over the weekend, resulting in nearly 2,400 arrests and almost 1,000 injured emergency workers, the French Interior Ministry said.
Demonstrators clashed with police, set fire to municipal buildings including a historic town hall in Limoges, and smashed windows during protests over living costs and school conditions.
French President Emmanuel Macron vowed on Sunday to take legal action and hold accountable those responsible for the violence.
body: Widespread violence erupted across France over the weekend, as rioters and looters ransacked storefronts, clashed with police and set fire to municipal buildings.
Nearly 2,400 people were arrested and almost 1,000 police officers and firefighters were injured, the French Interior Ministry said, after some of the worst unrest the country has seen in years.

In cities across the country, demonstrators set fire to newsstands and smashed windows. The violence followed weeks of largely peaceful protests over the cost of living and school conditions that expanded with an attempt to revive the “yellow vest” movement Saturday.
In Limoges, a town in central France, dramatic scenes emerged overnight Saturday as rioters broke into the historic town hall and set it ablaze.
Aerial images the following morning revealed the smoldering remains of the 19th century building, which had survived two world wars, capping one of the most violent days in France’s recent history.
Across the country in Lyon, southeastern France, an elderly man wearing a gas mask fled from tear gas at the Place des Terreaux on Saturday.
Crowds massed along the narrow streets of Paris throughout the weekend as masked demonstrators set up burning barricades near Place de la Republique, a major intersection through the city.
Striking scenes of disorder emerged from the French capital, including the monument at Place de la Republique where masked demonstrators burned flares and waved flags on Saturday.
Nearby, a man with a crucifix bearing the message “Love will triumph” rested near a burning vehicle in central Paris.
French President Emmanuel Macron on Sunday vowed legal action against those responsible for the violence. “Those who sought to bring down the Republic will be held accountable,” he said.

articles.headline: Australian prime minister says lawmaker critically injured by car is 'no accident'
keyFacts: Australian independent lawmaker Helen Haines was critically injured after being struck by a car outside her office.
Prime Minister Anthony Albanese stated that the collision was a deliberate act and not an accident.
Police arrested a 43-year-old driver at the scene and recovered a knife from the vehicle.
body: Australian prime minister says lawmaker critically injured by car is 'no accident'

MELBOURNE, Australia — A car hit an Australian federal independent lawmaker on Monday, critically injuring her in an apparent deliberate attack, Prime Minister Anthony Albanese said. The driver was arrested.
Helen Haines, 65, was struck by a Toyota Land Cruiser SUV outside her electoral district office mid afternoon in the city of Wangaratta in Victoria state, a police said.
Albanese said the national counterterrorism team, incorporating police and intelligence agencies, was investigating.
"This wasn't an accident. There was a deliberate act, it would appear. We don't know what the motivation is," Albanese told Australian Broadcasting Corp.
The 43-year-old driver was arrested at the scene by a passerby. He will be interviewed in relation to the incident, police said.
"A knife was located by police and seized from inside the Toyota," police said.
"At this stage, police are investigating as to whether this was an intentional act," police added.
Haines, who was first elected to the Parliament in 2019, was taken to a hospital with critical injuries, police said.

The episode has renewed safety concerns for Australian lawmakers, in a country where politicians have historically been highly accessible to the public and usually go about their business without security officers present. But public incitement against officials is growing.

Australian Federal Police Commissioner Krissy Barrett said in 2025 that threats against parliamentarians had doubled over the past three years. Police data showed more than 1,000 such threats against politicians in the 2025-2026 financial year, Home Affairs Minister Tony Burke said Monday.
Albanese told the ABC it was "unfortunate" that an increasingly polarized political climate had already led to security changes for Australia's lawmakers.

"I think there has been a rise in temperature and there has been too much shouting, not enough discourse, not enough polite conversation and disagreement," he said Monday. There was "no question" that social media played a part, Albanese added.

In Britain, murders of politicians have prompted bolstered security. Labour lawmaker Jo Cox was shot and stabbed in 2016 by a far-right extremist, and Conservative David Amess was stabbed in 2021 by an attacker inspired by the Islamic State group.
In July, the former politician and reality TV contestant Ann Widdecombe was found slain with a hammer at her home. A man has been charged with murder and terrorism-related offenses.
